extracted.subtask_short: evaluating patent eligibility of treatment claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating subject-matter eligibility of "method of treatment" patent claims under the Alice/Mayo framework in light of the Federal Circuit's decision in Vanda Pharmaceuticals v. West-Ward. Focuses on Step 2A (the "directed to" inquiry), claim-as-a-whole analysis, and related procedural handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the claims as a whole in Step 2A
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim is "directed to" a judicial exception, the claims must be evaluated as a whole, including any arguably conventional steps (e.g., genotyping and treatment steps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit evaluated the claims as a whole when determining that the claim was not "directed to" the recited natural relationship between genotype and QTc prolongation. Cases cited include Finjan and Core Wireless. Examiners should not isolate individual claim elements when doing the Step 2A 'directed to' analysis; include conventional steps in the overall assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-of-treatment claims that practically apply natural relationships are patent eligible under Step 2A
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are 'method of treatment' claims and that practically apply natural relationships should be considered patent eligible under Step 2A because they are applications of natural relationships rather than claims 'directed to' the natural relationship itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit held the Vanda claims patent eligible under Step 2A because they were 'directed to a method of using iloperidone to treat schizophrenia,' i.e., an application that 'confine[s] their reach to particular applications.' Examiners should treat such claims as applications of natural relationships rather than claims to the natural relationship per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish treatment-purpose steps from data-gathering/diagnostic steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether claimed steps (e.g., administering a drug) are performed to apply a natural relationship (treatment) or to gather data about the relationship (diagnosis); this distinction affects whether the claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memo contrasts Vanda with Mayo: in Mayo the administering step was performed to gather data and was ancillary to the diagnostic focus, so the claim as a whole was directed to a natural law; in Vanda the administering step required a treating doctor to administer the drug to treat disease, which supports finding the claim directed to an application. Examiners should assess the purpose/context of steps when classifying claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality/unconventionality of steps is not required for Step 2A eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary for 'method of treatment' claims that practically apply natural relationships to include nonroutine or unconventional steps in order to be considered patent eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 in the Step 2A 'directed to' inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit did not consider whether the treatment steps were routine or conventional when making its 'directed to' determination in Vanda. Thus, absence of non-routine steps does not alone make a method-of-treatment claim ineligible at Step 2A; non-routine analysis is part of Step 2B, which may be unnecessary if Step 2A is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim is eligible under Step 2A, do not perform Step 2B
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after evaluating the claim as a whole in Step 2A, the claim is determined not to be 'directed to' a judicial exception, there is no need to conduct the Step 2B (inventive concept) analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the claim in Vanda was determined eligible in the Step 2A 'directed to' part of the test, the Federal Circuit did not perform a Step 2B analysis. Examiners should stop the Alice/Mayo framework once Step 2A resolves eligibility in favor of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should 'confine their reach to particular applications' to be treated as applications rather than judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that confines its reach to a particular application (rather than broadly claiming a natural relationship) is more likely to be treated as an application of that relationship and thus not 'directed to' the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memo references the Supreme Court's distinction that method-of-treatment claims 'confine their reach to particular applications' and thus are not implicated by Mayo/Myriad. Examiners should consider whether claim scope limits the claim to a practical application (e.g., a treatment regimen tied to a particular patient genotype) when performing the Step 2A analysis.
